description: Stand on a step and lower one heel, slowly. Your heel drop number reveals the Achilles tendon, the biggest spring in your body. Learn why bouncing and stretching it are backwards, how the spring actually stores energy, and the slow eccentric protocol that rebuilds it.

scenes.narration: Stand on the edge of a step, one foot, heel hanging off the back. Rise up onto your toes using both feet if you need to, then lift the other foot away so one leg holds everything. Now lower that heel below the level of the step, taking a full FIVE SECONDS to get there. That is one rep. Count how many slow, smooth drops you can do on one leg before the heel starts rushing, shaking, or refusing. That number is your HEEL DROP TEST. It is not a calf test. It is a direct reading of the ACHILLES TENDON, the thickest, strongest spring in your body, and the way most people train it is exactly backwards. Write your number down. At the end I will show you what it means, and what to do instead.

scenes.label: SLOW ONE-LEG HEEL DROPS
scenes.narration: Here is the line. TWELVE slow drops per leg means your Achilles is loading and releasing like a spring under full control. Under six is where most people start, usually with a heel that free-falls the last part of the way down. Over fifteen, you own the kind of ankle spring that sprinters and jumpers are made of, and springs respond to training at any age.
scenes.sub: under 6: free-falling heel - 6 to 11: building - over 15: wired spring

lines: It stores energy when you land.
It returns it when you push off.
beats.title: THE FREE ENGINE

scenes.narration: The ACHILLES TENDON is the thickest tendon in your body, a band as wide as your thumb running from your calf muscles down to your heel bone. Its job is not to pull. Its job is to SPRING. Every step you take, the tendon stretches as your foot lands, storing elastic energy, then recoils as you push off, handing that energy back for free. Studies of running estimate the Achilles returns a large share of the energy of every stride, energy your muscles would otherwise have to pay for. That is why your heel drop was slow. A spring is only useful if it can load under control. When the heel free-falls, the spring is being dropped, not loaded, and a dropped spring stores nothing. The drop test measures whether you own the spring or the spring owns you. The Achilles has one more trick worth knowing. Its fibers spiral as they descend, rotating like a wrung towel, and that spiral lets the tendon store more energy and release it more smoothly than a straight band could. It also means the tendon is built to be loaded in its full length, from a deep stretch to a hard push-off, not babied in the middle ranges forever.

Here is the backwards part. Most guys train the Achilles with fast, bouncy calf raises, chasing a burn. But bouncing lets momentum and the stretch reflex do the work in a split second, far too fast for the tendon cells to register a building signal. The classic research on Achilles problems found the opposite approach works: ECCENTRIC loading, lowering the heel slowly under full tension, the exact movement in your test. When a muscle works while it lengthens, the tendon takes sustained, serious load, and sustained load is the language collagen understands. Slow drops are not the rehab version of calf training. They are the original version, the one the tissue was designed to answer. Bouncing is the remix, and the remix does not build springs. There is a dose detail in that classic research worth copying: the drops were done slowly, daily, for weeks, with load added gradually in a backpack. Nothing exotic. The magic was never the exercise. It was the patience wrapped around it.

beats.text: DEEP CALF WORKS THE LONG GAME

beats.label: OF THE TENDON'S LOAD IS DAILY LIFE

scenes.narration: One more layer. Two calf muscles feed this tendon: the GASTROCNEMIUS you can see, and the SOLEUS underneath it, a deep endurance muscle that works every second you stand. The soleus is the unsung partner in the spring, and it is trained best with the knee slightly bent, which is why a complete Achilles program includes straight-knee drops for the surface muscle and bent-knee drops for the deep one. And remember the scale of the job. You take thousands of steps a day, and the Achilles loads on every single one. This tendon does not need you to invent training for it. It needs you to upgrade the quality of the loading it already gets, a few slow, deliberate sets at a time.

Your advantage is control. A heel drop charges the spring with your full bodyweight on one leg. The heavier the body, the more that load overwhelms control, and the heel starts dropping instead of lowering. At your weight, you can keep every centimeter of the descent smooth and slow, which means every rep is a perfect signal. The heavy guy gets six sloppy drops. You get twelve clean ones, and clean is the only currency tendons accept. This is why light athletes so often own the best springs in the room. The spring does not care how much you weigh. It cares how honestly you load it.
Drop with me. One leg, five seconds down, forty seconds of work, twenty of rest, three rounds, switching legs each round. Use both feet to get back up. The lowering is the training. Go.

beats.text: LOAD IT, DO NOT ATTACK IT

scenes.narration: Now, stop doing it wrong. Wrong one: bouncing calf raises, all speed and burn, no signal. Wrong two: aggressive stretching of a cold Achilles, yanking on a spring you are about to ask for power. Wrong three: the all-or-nothing pattern, one huge session, then two weeks of nothing while the tendon forgets. Wrong four: running through morning stiffness and pain because a schedule said today is run day. Wrong five: training only straight knees and never the bent-knee position where the deep calf works. Doing it right looks almost too simple: slow heel drops, straight and bent knee, most days, progressing by control before load. Tendons this big remodel over months, and that is fine, because they also keep their gains for years. One rule above all: Achilles pain that changes how you walk, or pain that is still there after two sensible weeks, goes to a professional. Springs are precious. Get them inspected. Film one set from the side each week. Your heel will show you the truth about your control long before your feelings do, and the footage makes a brutally honest progress log.

scenes.label: RETEST THE HEEL DROP
scenes.narration: So, your number. Under SIX: your spring is being dropped, not loaded, and that is the most common starting point there is. Six to eleven: the control is arriving, and daily drops will move you quickly. Over TWELVE: your Achilles loads like a spring and releases like one too. Use the slower leg as your official number. Retest in thirty days, same step, same five-second rule. Put today's number in the comments. Just the number. Springs take weeks to build and the thread will prove it.
scenes.sub: same step, five seconds down, slower leg counts

scenes.narration: Your spring was never weak. It was being bounced instead of built. Give it thirty days of slow drops and bring me the new number. Subscribe, because next we test the whole ankle spring system with a hop test that does not forgive. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Stop Doing Achilles training Wrong: Train Your Achilles tendon Instead
